l: CRAG, HYBGRAG: Hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Textual and Relational Knowledge Bases
s: CRAG is a benchmark for end-to-end RAG performance, combining open-domain question answering and knowledge-base question answering. It provides knowledge graphs from five domains and a testing set of 1,335 textual and relational questions, including simple, comparison, and multi-hop types. Questions are classified by type, dynamism, and domain; topic entities and useful relations are extracted; and either text documents or a knowledge graph is selected as the reference source. For text retrieval, it uses question-based web search and ranks web pages with BAAI/bge-m3. For relational questions, its hybrid retrieval module is replaced with graph retrieval, which builds useful-relation ego-graphs and retrieves reasoning paths from topic entities. A router makes the first decision and can move to another ranked document batch when validation rejects the current output. The workflow proceeds through router reflection, validation, commenting, answer generation, and evaluation against a ground-truth answer. It uses chain-of-thought prompting for generator LLMs and Claude 3 Sonnet to label answers as accurate, incorrect or hallucinated, or missing. Because CRAG lacks retrieval ground truth, corrective feedback is constructed from router actions and evaluation. HYBGRAG, adapted to CRAG, is reported to outperform the listed baselines and achieve the best listed results with Llama 3.1 70B and Claude 3 Sonnet.

l: VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: The document presents VideoRAG, a retrieval-augmented generation framework that treats a video corpus as external knowledge. Rather than relying chiefly on text, images, or textual descriptions of videos, it dynamically retrieves videos relevant to a user query and generates answers grounded in both their visual and textual content. Its central motivation is that videos preserve temporal dynamics, spatial details, and multimodal cues that other RAG sources can miss. VideoRAG is enabled by Large Video Language Models, which represent and understand videos for retrieval and response generation. The pipeline retrieves query-relevant videos, uses adaptive frame selection to retain informative frames while reducing redundancy in long videos, and integrates selected visual material with available text. When subtitles or descriptions are unavailable, it uses automatic speech recognition to produce auxiliary transcripts. Frame-space reduction through clustering is also part of the approach. The evaluation builds question-answering data by linking WikiHowQA query-answer pairs with HowTo100M query-video pairs, alongside an automatically collected synthetic dataset. Across reported metrics, VideoRAG variants, especially VIDEORAG-V and VIDEORAG-VT, generally outperform textual, text-image, and text-video RAG baselines. Results indicate that visual features, textual features, and their combination improve retrieval and generation; adaptive frame selection benefits both; and larger LVLMs generally perform better. Human evaluation favors VIDEORAG-VT. Oracle retrieval results suggest that stronger video retrieval could yield further gains. A case study illustrates that retrieved video supports a detailed answer about baking cookies on a car dashboard. The document concludes that VideoRAG provides a more holistic video-based RAG system and that its experiments validate advantages over existing methods. It also notes limits: full-pipeline evaluation needs query-video-answer triples, but suitable datasets remain scarce. Future work includes developing and releasing benchmark datasets and improving frame selection. Finally, it warns that biased or harmful material in a video corpus, as well as biases inherited by LVLMs, can affect generated answers; practitioners should assess these risks and use measures such as bias detection and filtering. The work received support from several Korean government and institutional grant programs.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a strategy and generation framework that combines retrieval with generation. It retrieves query-relevant knowledge from external sources or corpora, supplies it to a foundation model, and generates answers grounded in that content, mitigating inaccurate or outdated parametric knowledge and improving factual accuracy. It has chiefly focused on text, often using sources such as Wikipedia; newer work also considers images or text-image pairs, while videos have largely been overlooked. Advanced approaches can use iterative retrieval-generation cycles. Recent expansion extends the external knowledge source from text and static images to videos, with video retrieval and response generation as components. Case-study results show RAG systems outperform a NAÏVE baseline and suggest videos can provide richer information than textual, text-image, or text-description-based alternatives. VideoRAG incorporates videos rather than only textual representations or assumed relevant videos, while RAG over videos requires evaluation with query, relevant-video, and ground-truth-answer triples.

l: VideoRAG, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: VideoRAG is a novel retrieval-augmented generation framework and video-based RAG approach that uses a large video corpus as an external knowledge source for answering user queries. It dynamically retrieves query-relevant videos, then grounds response generation in those videos by jointly using visual information, video frames, and textual information. Powered by Large Video Language Models, it processes video content within a unified framework rather than relying solely on frame-based or text-conversion approaches. Its pipeline combines video retrieval, adaptive frame selection, auxiliary text generation, and video-augmented response generation. Adaptive frame selection retains only the most informative subset of frames, improving processing effectiveness and efficiency. When subtitles are unavailable, automatic speech recognition generates textual transcripts; the VT variant jointly uses frames and transcripts. The framework requires triples of queries, relevant videos, and ground-truth answers for evaluation, and datasets are constructed by associating WikiHowQA with HowTo100M, including an automatically collected synthetic dataset. VideoRAG is evaluated on question-answering tasks and reported RAG benchmarks. Its variants outperform conventional textual, text-image, and text-video RAG baselines, including TEXTVIDEORAG, and results indicate gains from stronger video retrieval, adaptive frame selection, and larger LVLMs. The work presents itself as among the first to operationalize a full RAG pipeline over a video corpus. It also identifies future opportunities to improve effectiveness and efficiency. Its use may carry risks from problematic corpus examples and biases in LVLMs.

l: Large Video Language Models, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Large Video Language Models are multimodal language models built on Large Language Models that directly process video content. With vision and text encoders, they jointly represent visual frames and associated textual data, including temporal, spatial, and multimodal information. They power VideoRAG by representing videos for retrieval and integrating retrieved videos with queries during response generation. Their development extends from object and action detection to spatio-temporal analysis, event-sequence prediction, causal inference, and context-aware descriptions.

l: videos, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Videos are a rich, underutilized source of multimodal knowledge for RAG systems, representing contextual details through temporal dynamics, spatial details, and multimodal cues. As sequences of visual frames that may include subtitles, they can capture complex processes, context-dependent interactions, and non-verbal signals that static modalities may miss. Diverse, high-quality video data are available on YouTube, but videos can be long and redundant, making complete frame processing infeasible for LVLMs. VideoRAG addresses this by dynamically retrieving videos, selecting frames, and providing visual and textual information to a large video language model. This preserves multimodal richness more effectively than approaches that retrieve frames only from a preselected video or convert videos into text.

l: multimodal knowledge, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Multimodal knowledge, inherent in much real-world information, is a video strength for conveying contextual detail; its importance exposes a RAG research gap from limited use of images and other non-textual information.

l: queries, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Queries are textual information used by VideoRAG to retrieve relevant videos by comparison with video representations, then appended to selected multimodal content to guide response generation.

l: generation, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Generation produces responses from a query and retrieved videos or documents. It combines video frames, associated subtitles or other text, and the query as multimodal input to a large video language model, grounding answers in retrieved information. Some approaches further use iterative retrieval cycles or adapt retrieval-augmented generation to query complexity.

l: adaptive frame selection, VideoRAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation over Video Corpus
s: Adaptive frame selection is a mechanism and frame selection strategy for VideoRAG. It addresses long, redundant videos and limited context sizes by narrowing all frames in a video to a small, informative, computationally feasible subset rather than processing every frame or uniformly sampling frames. The model is trained to choose frames that maximize retrieval and generation performance while reducing the amount of video content processed. During generation, it uses the query to guide selection and chooses the subset with the highest score. By using only the most informative full frames, it improves the effectiveness and efficiency of video processing, retrieval, and generation, and outperforms uniform sampling. Further gains in effectiveness and efficiency are proposed as future work.

It is critical to RAG performance: oracle retrieval is strongest, suggesting retrieval can improve. Textual features consistently outperform visual features, though combining them helps. Its corpus may contain problematic examples that support biased or harmful responses.

s: selects documents [during the retrieval step] Retrieval selects documents relevant to a query from a large corpus by calculating their similarity to the query, using retrievers such as those described by Robertson et al., Jones, Karpukhin et al., and Izacard et al.

l: SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: This unit is a paper in Volume 1: Long Papers of the Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, held April 29–May 4, 2025. Titled “SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains,” it is by Ran Xu, Hui Liu, Sreyashi Nag, Zhenwei Dai, Yaochen Xie, Xianfeng Tang, Chen Luo, Yang Li, Joyce C. Ho, Carl Yang, and Qi He of Emory University and Amazon. The paper presents SimRAG, a self-training framework that adapts large language models for specialized-domain retrieval-augmented question answering in science, medicine, and computer science. SimRAG first conducts retrieval-oriented fine-tuning using general instruction, context-aware QA, and retrieval-related data. It then uses an unlabeled domain corpus: the same model generates candidate answers and questions, retrieves contexts, and applies round-trip-consistency filtering to retain pseudo-labeled question-answer tuples. These synthetic data are blended with general instruction and context-aware QA data for continued domain-adaptive training. The study evaluates SimRAG across 11 datasets, two backbone sizes, and three domains, including medical datasets from MIRAGE plus LiveQA and MedicationQA; scientific tasks from MMLU subsets, ARC-challenge, and SciQ; and CS-Bench. It compares GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama3-8B-Instruct, Gemma2-27B-Instruct, RAFT, EvidenceRAG, and SimRAG. Results show gains of 1.2%–8.6% over baselines; with Gemma2-27B, SimRAG approaches GPT-4 performance. Ablations find that both Stage-I retrieval-oriented fine-tuning and Stage-II self-synthesized tuples matter, while question diversity and filtering help further. Case studies show more relevant, self-contained, and challenging synthetic examples than Llama3-8B-it. Limitations include use of only one pseudo-labeling round, added training time, and the expense of stronger query generators. Research support came partly from the Emory Global Diabetes Center of the Woodruff Sciences Center at Emory University.

l: SimRAG, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: SimRAG is a self-improving retrieval-augmented generation and self-training approach for adapting large language models to specialized-domain question answering using unlabeled domain corpora. Its central idea is to jointly equip a model for question answering with context and question generation from context, then use the same model to create, filter, and learn from domain-specific synthetic data. The framework has two stages. In Stage-I, it applies retrieval-oriented fine-tuning on general-domain instruction-following, question-answering, and search-related data. In Stage-II, the Stage-I model extracts candidate answers from domain corpora, generates candidate questions and pseudo-labeled tuples, filters them through round-trip consistency to retain high-quality examples, and continuously fine-tunes on the resulting QA pairs for progressive self-improvement. Question filtering removes low-quality data and accelerates training; short-span question answering is among the generated question types. SimRAG supports multiple question-answering formats and is robust to DRAGON as an alternative retriever. It was evaluated on 11 datasets across biomedical, natural/social sciences, and computer science domains, with Llama3-8B-Instruct and Gemma2-27B-Instruct backbones. It consistently outperforms domain-specific LLMs, general-domain retrieval-augmented LMs, Llama3-8B-Instruct, and Gemma2-27B-Instruct in these domains, with reported gains of 1.2%–8.6%; using Gemma2-27B, it approaches GPT-4. Stage-II contributes materially: removing it lowers reported medical and scientific averages. SimRAG also has limitations involving pseudo-label refinement, added training time, and the choice of query generation models. The work was done during an internship at Amazon.

l: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: is_a Retrieval-Augmented Generation [self-improving] Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation is the approach identified in the title as being used to adapt large language models to specialized domains.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is a technique, tool, and question answering system that enhances large language models by integrating external knowledge for knowledge-intensive tasks. It supports question answering, language modeling, long-tail knowledge, and specialized-domain adaptation while avoiding costly retraining and reducing hallucination by grounding outputs in relevant evidence. In its typical approach, a retriever fetches supporting documents or contexts from a large corpus, and a generator or LLM produces answers from that retrieved context. Its development emphasizes dynamic retrieval to refine fetched content, filtering irrelevant contexts for robustness, and instruction fine-tuning to improve search and RAG capabilities. During medical evaluation, it is used at inference with top-10 retrieval results from multiple models; other datasets use top-10 passages fetched through Google Search.

l: Large Language Models, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Large Language Models are models with question-answering abilities that use external knowledge through retrieval-augmented generation. They can struggle with distribution shifts and accurately extracting information in specialized, domain-specific contexts. In SimRAG, a single Large Language Model is fine-tuned on instruction-following, question-answering, search-related, and general retrieval-oriented tasks; it then generates domain-relevant questions, candidate questions and answers, and answers from queries and retrieved contexts. Stage-II adapts it to specialized domains through synthetic data, supporting self-improvement and reducing data-generation costs.

l: specialized domains, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Specialized domains, including science and medicine, are target environments for adapting large language models and general-purpose RAG systems. They pose distribution-shift, domain-information, privacy, and scarce-label challenges. SimRAG studies biomedical, natural and social sciences, and computer science question answering, then uses each domain’s unlabeled corpus to generate synthetic training data for domain-adaptive fine-tuning.

l: question answering, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Question answering is a knowledge-intensive NLP task and the primary evaluation task for retrieval-augmented generation. SimRAG adapts large language models to domain-specific question answering by training on context, jointly supporting answer and question generation, and continuously fine-tuning on generated examples.

l: domain adaptation, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Domain adaptation is needed to address distribution shifts and limited access to domain-specific data when applying general-purpose retrieval-augmented generation systems to fields such as science and medicine. SimRAG performs this adaptation through self-generated, filtered training examples.

l: question generation, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Question generation is a SimRAG capability complementary to question answering: prompted with unlabeled, domain-specific context, it produces diverse grounded questions, reinforcing context-based answering.

l: unlabeled corpora, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Domain corpora provide the unlabeled specialized-domain material from which SimRAG generates grounded question-answer pairs. The corpora are used to specialize a model that has first learned general instruction-following, question answering, and question generation skills. The unlabeled corpus provides specialized-domain documents from which candidate answer spans and questions are generated. These documents also serve as potential supporting contexts during retrieval-based filtering.

l: pseudo-labeled training samples, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: This entity is pseudo-labeled training samples: synthetic domain-relevant question-answer examples containing a generated query, retrieved or source context, and a generated answer. They are generated from unlabeled specialized-domain corpora by SimRAG using a model fine-tuned after Stage-I. Samples span multiple task types and are filtered or denoised through quality checks, including retaining cases whose answers appear in top-k retrieved documents. Used for continuous Stage-II domain-adaptive fine-tuning, they improve domain-specific retrieval-augmented generation tasks. From generation through retrieval-based filtering to training, SimRAG’s samples are more relevant on average than examples from the backbone model or off-the-shelf T5-Large.

l: domain-specific question answering, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Domain-specific question answering is SimRAG’s target application, spanning medical, scientific, and computer science datasets and formats from multiple-choice to claim verification. SimRAG uses domain corpora to generate grounded question-answer examples, continues fine-tuning models, and improves results over baselines across 11 datasets by 1.2%–8.6%.

l: GPT-4-generated synthetic data, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: SimRAG uses GPT-4 to generate synthetic QA fine-tuning examples from unlabeled specialized-domain corpora, adding explicit quality control to address data scarcity and prior limitations.

l: GPT-4, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: GPT-4 is an off-the-shelf general-domain LLM, presented and used as a proprietary reference model. It is evaluated across medical, scientific, and computer-science domains, scoring 69.34, 82.51, and 70.34 overall respectively, and judges CS-Bench fill-in-the-blank and open-ended questions. With Gemma2-27B, SimRAG outperforms it on reported CS overall.

l: self-training, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Self-training, also called pseudo-labeling, is a semi-supervised learning method that refines large language models with synthetic examples from unlabeled corpora. A teacher model generates labels or pseudo-labeled query, context, and answer tuples; a student or fine-tuned LLM is then trained on the generated, filtered samples, progressively improving outputs. It is used for text classification, natural language understanding, ranking, instruction fine-tuning, reasoning, alignment, and domain-adaptive fine-tuning. Its major drawback is label noise, mitigated by sample selection and reweighting.

l: pseudo-labeled data, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: SimRAG generates pseudo-labeled question-answer data from unlabeled specialized-domain corpora using the same language model. It extracts candidate answers, generates conditioned questions, and filters tuples through round-trip consistency. After Stage-I, question and answer generation support continued fine-tuning; filtering improves performance and training speed, while diverse question types yield the strongest domain-specific question answering results.

l: round-trip consistency filtering, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Round-trip consistency filtering improves synthetic question-answer quality by retaining generated pairs or pseudo-labeled tuples only when retrieval returns the original context among top results; retained tuples include a question, documents, and an answer for further fine-tuning.

l: question, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: A query is used by the retriever to select relevant contexts, after which the LLM generates an answer. In Stage-II, queries are generated from candidate answers and their source documents.

l: answer, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: An answer is generated by the LLM from a query and its context. In Stage-II, candidate answer spans are first generated from documents and are then used as ground-truth answers for query generation.

l: computer science domain, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: The computer science domain is a specialized evaluation domain assessed with CS-Bench. It uses Wikipedia’s computer science subset and arXiv articles as source corpora for pseudo-labeled data, addressing limited computer-science coverage in the broader scientific domain. SimRAG scores 57.63 with an 8B backbone and 60.96 with 27B, improving on corresponding Llama and Gemma variants.

l: domain-specific LLMs, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Domain-specific LLMs typically rely on continuous pretraining or domain-specific fine-tuning. The unit notes that these models have received little focus for domain-specific retrieval-augmented generation settings.

l: retriever, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: The retriever selects top-k relevant contexts from a corpus for a query, supports retrieval-augmented generation with an LLM generator, and filters synthetic QA pairs during domain-adaptive fine-tuning.

l: pseudo-labeling, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Pseudo-labeling uses a teacher model to generate labels for fitting a student model and is one of the earliest approaches to semi-supervised learning. Its major drawback is vulnerability to label noise, which can be addressed through sample selection and reweighting.

l: two-stage fine-tuning framework, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: The two-stage fine-tuning framework in SimRAG first fine-tunes a model on retrieval-related data. It then performs domain-adaptive fine-tuning with self-training using pseudo-labeled examples filtered by round-trip consistency.

l: Stage-I training, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Stage-I training is a general-domain, retrieval-oriented fine-tuning stage that precedes Stage-II domain adaptive fine-tuning. It trains an instruction-tuned LLM on general supervised fine-tuning, general instruction, context-aware question-answering, and retrieval-related data to improve context use, answer generation, query generation, and domain-specific question answering. Using one epoch, AdamW, a 5e-7 learning rate, batch size 64, and gradient accumulation 8, it improves question-answering performance and produces higher-quality synthetic question-answer pairs.

l: domain adaptive fine-tuning with self-training, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Domain adaptive fine-tuning with self-training is the second stage of SimRAG. In this stage, the model extracts candidate answers from the corpus, generates candidate questions conditioned on documents and answers, and is further fine-tuned on the filtered pseudo-labeled examples.

l: instruction fine-tuning, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: computes_loss_on answer [exclusively on assistant response tokens] Instruction fine-tuning computes the loss only on assistant-response tokens for each training sample. It is used in Stage-I with general instruction, context-aware QA, and retrieval-related data.

l: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: is_a instruction fine-tuned LLM [used as an example backbone] Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct is given as an example of an instruction fine-tuned LLM used as a backbone.

l: Stage-II training, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Stage-II training is a domain adaptation stage that adapts the Stage-I model to specialized domains. It generates pseudo-labeled, self-synthesized training samples from unlabeled domain corpora, filters them for high-quality answerable QA pairs, and combines them with general instruction and context-aware QA data for continued fine-tuning. It uses batch size 64, gradient accumulation 8, and one epoch, with learning rates of 2e-7 for Llama3 and 5e-7 for Gemma. Diverse question types perform best; removing short-span QA hurts most. It further improves results after Stage-I, while removing it lowers medical and scientific performance.

l: supporting documents, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Supporting documents provide the evidence or context used by the LLM to answer a query. In the synthetic-data process, documents from the specialized corpus ground candidate answers and generated questions.

l: context, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: A context is a retrieved document or set of documents supplied to the LLM for answer generation. Stage-I includes context-aware QA training, and Stage-II filters samples according to whether the answer occurs in retrieved contexts.

l: General Instruction Fine-tuning data, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: General Instruction Fine-tuning data helps preserve the model's ability to comprehend and follow instructions. It includes OpenAssistant, Dolly, SODA, ELI5, Self-Instruct, and Unnatural Instructions.

l: General domain Context-aware QA data, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: General domain Context-aware QA data trains the LLM to generate accurate answers grounded in relevant contexts. It includes datasets such as DROP, NQ, Squad, NarrativeQA, Quoref, ROPES, Open-bookQA, LogiQA, TAT-QA, WebGLM, StrategyQA, BoolQ, FaVIQ, and FEVER.

l: General Retrieval-related Data, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: General Retrieval-related Data is retrieval-related data used to improve answer and query generation, developing answer-generation from grounding documents and query-generation from answers and documents for high-quality pseudo-labeled samples.

l: Dragon, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Dragon is a strong retriever for generated QA filtering: it retrieves top-k documents for generated queries, retains pairs whose answers appear there, and extends context length as an alternative retriever for SimRAG and baselines.

l: claim verification, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: uses context [to support or refute a generated claim] Claim verification is one of the diverse question types generated in Stage-II. It bypasses candidate answer generation and instead produces a claim that the document can support or refute.

l: data filtering, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Data filtering keeps only high-quality synthetic QA pairs that are answerable using the top-k documents retrieved for their generated queries. The filtering criterion requires the generated answer to be present in those documents.

l: Experimental Setup, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: Experimental Setup evaluates models across 11 medical, scientific, and computer science datasets, defines task-specific metrics, compares baseline groups, and reports experiments using 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs.

l: medical domain, SimRAG: Self-Improving Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Adapting Large Language Models to Specialized Domains
s: The medical domain is a specialized evaluation domain covering five MIRAGE benchmark datasets plus LiveQA and MedicationQA. Stage-II pseudo-labeled samples use Textbooks, Wikipedia, and PubMed, while evaluation uses top-10 MIRAGE retrieval context. l: CLERC: A Dataset for U. S. Legal Case Retrieval and Retrieval-Augmented Analysis Generation
s: The document presents CLERC (Case Law Evaluation and Retrieval Corpus), a dataset built with legal professionals from U.S. federal case law in CAP through September 21, 2021, to support systems that assist legal writing. It contains 25.5 million instances and targets three connected tasks: legal document retrieval, passage retrieval, and retrieval-augmented legal analysis generation. The central practical setting is lawyers drafting motions and briefs by finding relevant precedent, citing it, and synthesizing cited authority into analysis supporting a reasoning goal. CLERC is prepared in forms including CLERC/doc, CLERC/passage, and CLERC/generation. Documents are concatenated, passages chunked, and analytical paragraphs selected. Retrieval queries are created from 300-word contexts by removing central citations or all citations, with direct and indirect query types distinguished. Generation inputs combine prior case context with salient passages from cited cases. An example query concerns summary judgment and cites Fed.R.Civ.P. 56(c), Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, and Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. The document places CLERC among prior work on legal retrieval and generation, long-context generation, and long-document retrieval, arguing that existing benchmarks do not sufficiently test BERT-based and long-context models on clearly defined legal retrieval tasks. Experiments show substantial shortcomings. BM25 surpasses zero-shot late-interaction and bi-encoder retrieval models, while fine-tuned DPR models, especially a LegalBERT-based model, perform better. Still, zero-shot IR reaches only 48.3% recall@1000, and performance varies with query type, length, and domain shift. Repeated legal terms and non-central citations can distract retrievers. For generation, supplying texts of cited cases improves citation coverage, precision, and hallucination-related measures, but outputs remain factually and analytically limited. GPT-4o obtains the highest ROUGE F-scores while hallucinating the most. The document further argues that citation metrics alone can be misleading, illustrated with Llama-3-8B, and proposes adapting FActScore for legal factual recall. The work concludes that CLERC is an initial interdisciplinary step toward legal-assistance systems, but current systems, including fine-tuned ones, are not yet suitable for these tasks. It notes possible OCR errors in CAP data and warns that historical case law can carry racism, sexism, and other harmful ideologies that legal intelligence systems may propagate.

s: CLERC, the Case Law Evaluation and Retrieval Corpus, is a colossal dataset of historical U.S. federal case law, built with legal professionals for training and evaluating models. It supports two backbone tasks: information retrieval, including case and legal citation retrieval, and retrieval-augmented legal analysis generation. The records present a summary-judgment query with citation masking, including single-removed views that mask a central citation and salient sentence and all-removed views that mask all citations while retaining statutory references.
